newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa heads for clash with mines on environment.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa heads for clash with mines on environment.

text.p: South Africa's Ministry of Environmental Affairs and Tourism is heading for conflict over its plans to classify mining as an activity dangerous to the environment.
Minister Pallo Jordan announced plans this week for new rules requiring all new mining applications by law to be subject to environmental impact assessments (EIA).

"If mining is identified as an activity that has a substantial detrimental effect on the environment, all new mining applications will then be subject to environmental impact assessments," the ministry said.

The Chamber of Mines employer body told Reuters companies were already obliged to do environmental management programme reports (EMPR) under the 1992 Mining and Minerals Act and that the proposed new legislation was unfair.

"We would be the last people to say that mining has no impact on the environment. But mining already does its own EMPRs and it is unfair and clumsy to duplicate the law," said John Kilani, environmental affairs advisor to the Chamber of Mines.
But sources close to the ministry say mining has for too long enjoyed a privileged position.

"We've got very strong mineral laws and rights for very good reasons. For many years our economy was run on this. It is very deeply entrenched, and perhaps the industry has been a little bit spoilt," one source said.

Since its appointment after the country's first democratic all-race elections in April 1994, the Environmental Affairs Ministry and its partner the Water Affairs and Forestry Ministry have halted a number of mining projects.

"I think the current ministry is more pro-active. The minister (Jordan) is really committed to apply legislation where he can. We are making progress," said Environmental Affairs spokesman Wynand Fourie.
Last October the ministry prevented diamond prospecting in the Madimbu Corridor, an 80 km strip along the banks of the Limpopo River bordering Zimbabwe.

In May 1996 the Water Affairs and Forestry Ministry instructed Randgold and Exploration Co Ltd's Grootvlei Proprietary Mines Ltd to stop pumping contaminated underground water into a wetland east of Johannesburg.
And the cabinet last March rejected plans by a joint venture of Gencor Ltd and RTZ Corp to mine for titanium on the eastern shore of the St Lucia estuary near the Mozambique border.
Nonetheless, Fourie said the ministry wanted to avoid over-regulation.
"We would like to avoid unneccessary investigations to be undertaken. Government doesn't want to over-regulate. It also wants to stimulate growth and development," he said.

Kilani said the mining industry had no objection to being classified as an activity considered detrimental to the environment but it wanted a clause to the proposed legislation that made it clear mining performed EMPRs already.
